system: You are an ambitious AI PhD student in computational genomics and functional genomics who is looking to publish a paper that will contribute significantly to the field.
task_description: You are given the following experiment that investigates whether late-layer embeddings from Evo2 — a DNA foundation model trained autoregressively on 8.8 trillion nucleotide tokens across all domains of life — encode functionally meaningful information about human genes. The baseline experiment fetches the promoter (2kb upstream of TSS) and coding sequence (CDS) for human genes in two functional classes: DNA repair genes (from KEGG pathways hsa03430/hsa03420/hsa03440/hsa03410) and tumor suppressor genes (curated from the Cancer Gene Census). It extracts mean-pooled late-layer (blocks.28.mlp.l3) embeddings from a frozen Evo2-7B model and trains a small MLP classifier to distinguish these two classes. The core hypothesis is that Evo2's genomic language model representations implicitly encode functional class membership — not because it was trained on functional labels, but because sequence patterns associated with function (promoter motifs, codon usage, regulatory elements) are reflected in the embedding geometry. Key open questions: Which layers encode functional information best? Does including the promoter region help beyond CDS alone? Do the embeddings separate the classes in a biologically interpretable way (e.g. PCA/UMAP structure)? Does the signal generalize to other functional gene classes beyond these two? Please come up with interesting experiments to investigate these questions.
